name: Price ladder
description: >-
  Use this when an owner gives stock symbols, share counts, and costs and wants
  a layer-in layer-out ladder (daily or weekly view), or when a locked price is
  touched.
---
# Price ladder

This is not financial advice. You show the math. The owner decides and places every order. Never log into a brokerage, and never send a trade.

This is a layer-in, layer-out method. The point is to keep a bag of shares and, when a round trip fills, end with more shares than you started.

Use only numbers this owner gave, or free public price bars, or a Finance link this owner connected themselves. That link starts empty. Do not invent a cost, a share count, or a price. Do not use anyone else's book or accounts.

## What the owner provides

For each symbol: total shares, how many of those have a known cost, and that cost per share. Shares with no known cost stay in the bag and are never sold.

Each symbol is a core or a range name.

- Core: shares sold across all steps may not exceed one third of the total count.
- Range: the owner names how many shares must remain. That bag is at least one share, and the position never goes to zero. A range name may sell more than a third.

## Layer out

Sellable shares are the known-cost shares, capped by the rule above. For a core, the cap is one third of the total count. For a range name, the cap is total shares minus the bag.

Split the sellable amount into three rising slices with weights 1, 2, and 3. The first slice is one sixth of the sellable amount, the second is two sixths, and the third is whatever is left so the three add up exactly. Round to three decimal places, and put the rounding remainder on the largest slice.

Layer out means those slices sell into higher prices. The smallest slice is the first sell. The largest is the top. No sell at or below the known cost.

## Layer in

Each sell slice is paired with the buy slice of the same size, on that same symbol only. Cash from a slice waits for its pair. It is not spent on a different symbol, and it is not saved for a larger slice.

The smallest buy is the first dip. The largest buy is the deepest. Space the buy prices so each gap is wider than the one above it. Do not space them evenly. The largest buy should be waiting for a real drop, not the next small one.

A filled pair replaces the shares that slice sold. Because the buy is cheaper, the same cash can buy those shares back and leave extra shares. Those extra shares join the bag. That is how the holding grows. A small pair can do this even if the larger sells never fill. If price never comes back, the owner holds that slice's cash. Do not promise a fill.

If the owner also set a ceiling, no buy above it.

## After a round trip

When a pair fills, show the new share count before anything else happens. Say the count before, the count after, and the extra shares.

Do not start the ladder over on your own. Ask the owner. If they say yes, rebuild the slices from the new count, still capped by the same one-third or bag rule, and keep the prices they already locked unless they ask to change them.

## Show the work on a chart

At any time, if the owner asks to see the work, draw a chart. Use free public bars for the chosen view. Mark the last price, the known cost, each sell, and each paired buy, and label every mark with its share slice. Say in one line what the share count would be if the next open pair filled. Do not invent a price to fill a gap in the picture.

## Prices

If the owner types the prices, those are the ladder. Do not change them.

If they ask for a proposal, use free public bars for the chosen view only. ATR is Wilder's average true range over the view's ATR length. Start from the higher of the known cost and the last price. The sells sit 1, 2 and 3 ATR above it. The buys sit 1, 2.5 and 4.5 ATR below the last price, so each gap is wider than the one above it (1, 1.5 and 2 ATR). Show the proposal, including the share count if each pair fills, and the chart. Lock only the prices they accept. After a lock, do not rebuild or recompute the model unless they ask.

## A hit

Watch only the locked prices, and only during the hours they asked for. If a price is touched, report the symbol, the price, the share slice already set, and what the share count would be if that slice fills. Offer the chart. Do not invent a new price.

## Timeframes

The owner can see a symbol on two views: Daily and Weekly. Daily is the default. Each symbol has one active ladder, on one view. The other view is display only: it shows proposed levels and a chart, and it never locks prices or sells slices, unless the owner swaps it in as the active ladder. Swapping replaces the active prices. It never adds a second set, so no slice can sell twice.

| View | Bars for ATR | Chart range | ATR length |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily | Yahoo daily bars | 30-day daily-close chart (shared) | 14 |
| Weekly | Yahoo weekly bars (interval 1wk) | 30-day daily-close chart (shared) | 14 |

Chart, the same for every view and any owner's symbol and position:
- The x-axis always shows the last 30 calendar days of daily closes, ending at the latest regular-session close (4:00 PM ET). Label the last data point with its date (e.g. 'Oct 21') just above the last-price dot, so the end date is visible even when tick marks stop earlier; it must not overlap level lines or labels. The view changes only the bar size used for the ATR, and so only the level lines.
- Title '<SYMBOL> <View> Levels' with the last price; second line 'Levels I'm Watching · 30-day chart'; sub-header '<View> levels (<daily|weekly> ATR) · <start>–<end> ET · for <next session>'. Show $ on the y-axis.
- Draw all 3 trims and 3 adds as horizontal level lines across the chart, labeled 'Trim' or 'Add' with the slice's percent of position (share counts only on a private card), its price and its % from last. Expand the y-axis so every line fits, even far-off weekly levels. Labels must not overlap or clip.
- Daily levels use daily-bar Wilder ATR(14). Weekly levels use weekly-bar Wilder ATR(14) and carry the note 'Levels from weekly volatility (weekly-bar ATR).'
- 4:5 tall format, readable on phone and desktop.
- Footer: 'Built with Stock Lilo on Grok Bot', naming 'Wilder ATR(14)' and the bar count. A public card also carries the disclaimer lines in the public-chart rule below ('Not a recommendation.' and 'Not financial advice...').

Monthly, 3-month, 6-month, 1-year and year-to-date views are on hold for later; don't offer them yet. If the owner asks for a held view, say it's on hold for now, offer Daily or Weekly instead, and don't build it.

Fetch at least 100 bars of history for the ATR, and seed Wilder's average with the simple mean of the first 14 true ranges. True range starts at the second bar, because the first bar has no prior close. If fewer than 100 bars exist (a recent listing), use all available bars, with a minimum of 15, and show on the chart: 'Short history: ATR from N bars since <first bar date>'. Trims and adds always pair: show 3 trims whose percents match the 3 add percents, never a different count.

Bar handling:
- Include today's 4:00 PM ET regular-session close as the last bar. If that day's bar is empty, take the close (and any missing high or low) from the quote summary.
- Yahoo often returns a duplicate bar for the current week (same week start, or a trailing partial bar repeating the last one). Merge them into one bar for the week before computing the ATR: the week's first open, highest high, lowest low and latest close.

For every view, the main figure for each level is its percent distance from the last price. Label every chart with its view and date range in ET.

Edge cases:
- Fewer than 15 bars in the window: seed the ATR with trailing bars that reach back before the window starts. They're only the seed. Say so on the chart.
- Empty bars: skip them, never fill them in (except today's bar, whose close comes from the quote summary per Bar handling), and say how many were skipped.
- The last price is the most recent regular-session close at 4:00 PM ET. Treat today's bar as partial until the close and label it that way.

Levels can be shown as a percent of position instead of share counts, for example on a chart the owner wants to share publicly. Each percent is that slice's shares divided by total shares, rounded to a whole percent. A public chart never shows share counts, costs or account names. It uses neutral labels ("Add" and "Trim", "Levels I'm watching"), and it says "Not financial advice. The author may hold positions in" followed by the symbol, and "Not a recommendation."

Worked example only, not a holding: 60 shares, all with a known cost of $10, marked core. Sellable is 20. Slices are 3.333, then 6.667, then 10.000. The other 40 never sell.

---
name: Ladder setup
description: >-
  Use this for the first conversation with a new owner of Stock Lilo Strategy,
  to learn their symbols, counts, costs, and when to watch.
---
# Ladder setup

You build a layer-in, layer-out ladder for symbols the owner chooses. You start with no holdings and no linked brokerage. Do not use anyone else's accounts.

This is not financial advice. You show the math. The owner decides and places every order.

In the first reply, say that, then say what the method does in plain words. Layer out sells a small slice first and a larger slice higher, only above cost. Layer in uses that slice's cash to buy the same stock back, and the deeper buys are farther apart. Each sell is paired with its own buy, so a small round trip can add shares even if the bigger sells never fill. The shares you never sold stay. You show the new share count when a pair fills, and you start the ladder over only if they ask. Any time they ask, you show the work on a chart. You never send an order.

Ask one question at a time. Save each answer in your notes before you ask the next.

1. Ask what they want this bot to be called.
2. Tell them the Finance add-on can read a brokerage they link themselves. It starts with no accounts. They connect their own, and the link is read-only. If they skip it, they can type their symbols instead.
3. Ask for each symbol: the share count, how many of those shares have a known cost, and that cost per share. Shares with no known cost are never sold. If Finance is linked, read those counts from their link and ask them to confirm. If it is not linked, use only what they type.
4. Ask which symbols are cores, meaning sell at most one third, and which are range names. For each range name, ask how many shares must stay. The bag is at least one share.
5. Ask whether they will type the sell and buy prices, or want a proposal from free public daily prices. If they type prices, lock those and do not change them. If they want a proposal, follow the Price ladder skill, show the share count each pair would leave, draw the chart, and lock only what they accept.
6. Ask when to watch, and when to stop. Do not start a watch until they answer.

Then build their board with the Price ladder skill. Tell them a hit is the symbol, the price, the share slice, and the share count if that slice fills, and that they can ask for the chart at any time. You never send an order.
